16.6

Mass, moments, centre of mass, inertia

Quiz 8

A metal plate with heavy and light spots. Its mass is density piled over the region. Its centre of mass is where you'd stick a pin so it sits level — the average position, with heavy bits voting harder.

mass and moments m=∬Rρ dAMy=∬Rx ρ dAMx=∬Ry ρ dAm = \iint_R \rho\,dA \qquad M_y = \iint_R x\,\rho\,dA \qquad M_x = \iint_R y\,\rho\,dAm=∬R​ρdAMy​=∬R​xρdAMx​=∬R​yρdA
centre of mass xˉ=Mym=1m∬Rx ρ dAyˉ=Mxm=1m∬Ry ρ dA\bar x = \frac{M_y}{m} = \frac{1}{m}\iint_R x\,\rho\,dA \qquad\qquad \bar y = \frac{M_x}{m} = \frac{1}{m}\iint_R y\,\rho\,dAxˉ=mMy​​=m1​∬R​xρdAyˉ​=mMx​​=m1​∬R​yρdA
moments of inertia — distance is SQUARED Ix=∬Ry2ρ dAIy=∬Rx2ρ dAI0=∬R(x2+y2)ρ dA=Ix+IyI_x = \iint_R y^2\rho\,dA \qquad I_y = \iint_R x^2\rho\,dA \qquad I_0 = \iint_R (x^2+y^2)\rho\,dA = I_x + I_yIx​=∬R​y2ρdAIy​=∬R​x2ρdAI0​=∬R​(x2+y2)ρdA=Ix​+Iy​

Naming trap

MyM_yMy​ uses xxx, and MxM_xMx​ uses yyy. The subscript names the axis you are taking the moment about, not the variable in the integrand. Same crossover in IxI_xIx​, which uses y2y^2y2 — distance from the xxx-axis is ∣y∣|y|∣y∣.

Algorithm · any of these quantities

  1. Set up the region once — limits, and polar if it's round.
  2. Pick the weight from the table: 111 for mass, xxx or yyy for a moment, x2+y2x^2+y^2x2+y2 for polar inertia.
  3. Integrate ∬(weight)ρ dA\iint(\text{weight})\rho\,dA∬(weight)ρdA. Every quantity in this section is that one integral with a different sticker.
  4. For a centre of mass, divide by mmm at the very end. Moments are not divided; centres of mass are.

Symmetry shortcut: if the region and the density are both symmetric about a line, the centre of mass lies on that line. That can kill half the work.

Uniform density? ρ\rhoρ is a constant, so it factors out of the top and bottom of xˉ\bar xxˉ and cancels completely. The answer is then called the centroid and depends only on the shape.

Check yourself

  1. Write xˉ\bar xxˉ for a lamina.

    Answer
    xˉ=1m∬Rx ρ dA\bar x=\dfrac1m\displaystyle\iint_R x\,\rho\,dAxˉ=m1​∬R​xρdA — the moment, divided by the mass.

  2. Why is moment of inertia weighted by distance squared?

    Answer
    Because it measures resistance to spinning, and mass far from the axis resists far more than mass near it.
16.7

Change of variables & the Jacobian

bonus · not on the plan

Purdue’s 37 lessons skip 16.7 — the plan jumps straight from mass calculations (16.6) to vector fields (17.1). Read this only if you want to see where the rrr and ρ2sin⁡φ\rho^2\sin\varphiρ2sinφ actually come from.

Bend the coordinate grid into whatever shape makes your region a plain rectangle. The bending stretches areas, so you owe a correction factor — and the Jacobian is exactly that factor.

the Jacobian determinant ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=∣∂x∂u∂x∂v∂y∂u∂y∂v∣dA=∣∂(x,y)∂(u,v)∣ du dv\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix}\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v}\\[8pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v}\end{vmatrix} \qquad\qquad dA = \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\,du\,dv∂(u,v)∂(x,y)​=​∂u∂x​∂u∂y​​∂v∂x​∂v∂y​​​dA=​∂(u,v)∂(x,y)​​dudv
change of variables ∬Rf(x,y) dA=∬Sf(x(u,v), y(u,v))∣∂(x,y)∂(u,v)∣du dv\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \iint_S f\bigl(x(u,v),\,y(u,v)\bigr)\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|du\,dv∬R​f(x,y)dA=∬S​f(x(u,v),y(u,v))​∂(u,v)∂(x,y)​​dudv

Algorithm · change of variables

  1. Choose uuu and vvv from the boundary. If the region is bounded by x+y=1x+y=1x+y=1, x+y=3x+y=3x+y=3, x−y=0x-y=0x−y=0, x−y=2x-y=2x−y=2, then take u=x+yu=x+yu=x+y, v=x−yv=x-yv=x−y — the region becomes the rectangle 1≤u≤31\le u\le31≤u≤3, 0≤v≤20\le v\le 20≤v≤2.
  2. Invert to get x(u,v)x(u,v)x(u,v) and y(u,v)y(u,v)y(u,v).
  3. Compute the Jacobian and take its absolute value.
  4. Rewrite the integrand in uuu and vvv.
  5. Integrate over the new, rectangular region.

Shortcut: if inverting is ugly, compute ∂(u,v)∂(x,y)\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}∂(x,y)∂(u,v)​ instead and use ∂(x,y)∂(u,v)=1/∂(u,v)∂(x,y)\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = 1\Big/\dfrac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}∂(u,v)∂(x,y)​=1/∂(x,y)∂(u,v)​.

Polar and spherical were Jacobians all along

For x=rcos⁡θ, y=rsin⁡θx=r\cos\theta,\ y=r\sin\thetax=rcosθ, y=rsinθ the Jacobian works out to exactly rrr. For spherical it works out to exactly ρ2sin⁡φ\rho^2\sin\varphiρ2sinφ. The rules you were told to memorise in 16.3 and 16.5 are just this one theorem, already applied.

Check yourself

  1. What is the Jacobian for polar coordinates?

    Answer
    Exactly rrr — the rule you memorised in 16.3 was this theorem all along.
UNIT 04

Vector calculus

Ch. 17 · Quizzes 8–10 → Midterm 2 → Final

One last new object: instead of a number at every point, an arrow at every point. Then four theorems that all say the same sentence — what happens on the edge equals what the derivative does inside. Lessons 25–33 finish Exam 2; Stokes and the divergence theorem (34–37) appear only on the Final.

17.1

Vector fields

Quiz 8

Wind, current, gravity, magnetic pull. Two questions decide everything that follows: does the wind go around, and does the wind go out?

a vector field F(x,y)=P(x,y) i+Q(x,y) jF(x,y,z)=P i+Q j+R k\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j \qquad\quad \mathbf F(x,y,z) = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j + R\,\mathbf kF(x,y)=P(x,y)i+Q(x,y)jF(x,y,z)=Pi+Qj+Rk

Gradient fields are the special ones: F=∇f\mathbf F = \nabla fF=∇f for some scalar fff. Physically, fff is a hill (or a potential) and F\mathbf FF points the way water would run. Section 17.3 is entirely about spotting these.

Check yourself

  1. What does divergence measure?

    Answer
    Net outflow from a tiny box: faucet if positive, drain if negative.

  2. What does curl measure?

    Answer
    Local spin — whether a paddlewheel turns. Not whether the flow curves: straight flow that is faster on one side still spins it.
17.2

Line integrals

Quiz 9

Walk a curve and add something up as you go. If the something is a height you get a curtain's area. If it's a push you get work.

scalar line integral — with respect to arc length ∫Cf ds=∫abf(r(t)) ∣r′(t)∣ dt\int_C f\,ds = \int_a^b f\bigl(\mathbf r(t)\bigr)\,\bigl|\mathbf r'(t)\bigr|\,dt∫C​fds=∫ab​f(r(t))​r′(t)​dt

Now the vector version. Wind straight at your back: full help. Wind from the side: does nothing. Wind in your face: fights you. Only the part of the push along your walk counts.

work — three notations for one integral ∫CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t) dt=∫CP dx+Q dy+R dz\int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \int_a^b \mathbf F\bigl(\mathbf r(t)\bigr)\cdot\mathbf r'(t)\,dt = \int_C P\,dx + Q\,dy + R\,dz∫C​F⋅dr=∫ab​F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫C​Pdx+Qdy+Rdz

Algorithm · evaluate any line integral

  1. Parametrize CCC. Line segment from AAA to BBB: r(t)=(1−t)A+tB\mathbf r(t) = (1-t)A + tBr(t)=(1−t)A+tB, 0≤t≤10\le t\le10≤t≤1. Circle of radius aaa: ⟨acos⁡t,asin⁡t⟩\langle a\cos t, a\sin t\rangle⟨acost,asint⟩. Graph y=g(x)y=g(x)y=g(x): ⟨t,g(t)⟩\langle t, g(t)\rangle⟨t,g(t)⟩.
  2. Compute r′(t)\mathbf r'(t)r′(t). For a scalar integral you also need ∣r′(t)∣|\mathbf r'(t)|∣r′(t)∣.
  3. Substitute the parametrization into F\mathbf FF or fff so everything is in terms of ttt alone.
  4. Dot (vector version) or multiply by ∣r′∣|\mathbf r'|∣r′∣ (scalar version).
  5. Integrate over the parameter range. If CCC is made of several pieces, do each separately and add.

Orientation trap

∫−CF⋅dr=−∫CF⋅dr\displaystyle\int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = -\int_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r∫−C​F⋅dr=−∫C​F⋅dr — reversing the walk flips the sign of work. But ∫−Cf ds=∫Cf ds\displaystyle\int_{-C} f\,ds = \int_C f\,ds∫−C​fds=∫C​fds — a curtain has the same area no matter which way you walk along its base. Vector integrals care about direction; scalar ones don't.

Check yourself

  1. What does ∫Cf ds\int_C f\,ds∫C​fds give when f=1f=1f=1?

    Answer
    The length of the curve.

  2. You walk CCC backwards. What happens to ∫CF⋅dr\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r∫C​F⋅dr?

    Answer
    The sign flips. But ∫Cf ds\int_C f\,ds∫C​fds does not change — a curtain has the same area either way.
17.3

Conservative fields & the FTLI

Quiz 9

Climb from the car park to the summit. Take the switchbacks or take the ridge — you gained exactly the same height. Some fields are just "downhill from a hill", and for those the route is irrelevant.

fundamental theorem for line integrals ∫C∇f⋅dr=f(r(b))−f(r(a))=f(end)−f(start)\int_C \nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r = f\bigl(\mathbf r(b)\bigr) - f\bigl(\mathbf r(a)\bigr) = f(\text{end}) - f(\text{start})∫C​∇f⋅dr=f(r(b))−f(r(a))=f(end)−f(start)

This is the FTC from Calc I wearing a coat: integrate a derivative, get boundary values. The whole path collapses to two evaluations.

Four ways of saying the same thing

F\mathbf FF is conservative ⟺ F=∇f\mathbf F = \nabla fF=∇f for some potential fff ⟺ ∫CF⋅dr\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r∫C​F⋅dr is path-independent ⟺ ∮CF⋅dr=0\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = 0∮C​F⋅dr=0 around every closed loop. On a simply connected region these are also equivalent to curl⁡F=0\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = \mathbf 0curlF=0.

the test 2-D: ∂P∂y=∂Q∂x3-D: curl⁡F=∇×F=0\text{2-D: } \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} \qquad\qquad \text{3-D: } \operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = \nabla\times\mathbf F = \mathbf 02-D: ∂y∂P​=∂x∂Q​3-D: curlF=∇×F=0

Algorithm · find the potential function fff

  1. Test first. Check Py=QxP_y = Q_xPy​=Qx​ (2-D) or curl⁡F=0\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F=\mathbf 0curlF=0 (3-D). If it fails, stop — there is no fff.
  2. Integrate PPP with respect to xxx: f=∫P dx+g(y,z)f = \displaystyle\int P\,dx + g(y,z)f=∫Pdx+g(y,z). The constant of integration is a function of the other variables, not a number.
  3. Differentiate your fff with respect to yyy and set it equal to QQQ. Solve for gyg_ygy​.
  4. Integrate gyg_ygy​ in yyy, picking up a new constant h(z)h(z)h(z).
  5. Repeat with zzz and RRR to pin down h(z)h(z)h(z). Add a genuine constant CCC at the end.
  6. Verify: ∇f\nabla f∇f should give back F\mathbf FF exactly.

Then use it: ∫CF⋅dr=f(end)−f(start)\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = f(\text{end}) - f(\text{start})∫C​F⋅dr=f(end)−f(start), and the parametrization never gets written down.

Worked example

F=⟨2xy, x2+2y⟩\mathbf F = \langle 2xy,\ x^2+2y\rangleF=⟨2xy, x2+2y⟩, from (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) to (1,3)(1,3)(1,3).

test

Py=2xP_y = 2xPy​=2x, Qx=2xQ_x = 2xQx​=2x ✓ conservative

step 2

f=∫2xy dx=x2y+g(y)f = \int 2xy\,dx = x^2y + g(y)f=∫2xydx=x2y+g(y)

step 3

fy=x2+g′(y)=x2+2y⇒g′(y)=2y⇒g=y2f_y = x^2 + g'(y) = x^2+2y \Rightarrow g'(y)=2y \Rightarrow g = y^2fy​=x2+g′(y)=x2+2y⇒g′(y)=2y⇒g=y2

potential

f=x2y+y2f = x^2y + y^2f=x2y+y2

evaluate

f(1,3)−f(0,0)=(3+9)−0=12f(1,3)-f(0,0) = (3+9) - 0 = \mathbf{12}f(1,3)−f(0,0)=(3+9)−0=12 — no parametrization needed.

Trap

Curl zero is not enough on a region with a hole. The classic F=⟨−yx2+y2, xx2+y2⟩\mathbf F = \left\langle \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2},\ \frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\right\rangleF=⟨x2+y2−y​, x2+y2x​⟩ passes Py=QxP_y=Q_xPy​=Qx​ everywhere it is defined, yet a loop around the origin gives 2π2\pi2π, not 0. The region must be simply connected — no punctures.

Check yourself

  1. What is the 2-D test for a conservative field?

    Answer
    ∂P∂y=∂Q∂x\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}=\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}∂y∂P​=∂x∂Q​ — and the region must have no holes.

  2. F\mathbf FF is conservative. What is ∮CF⋅dr\oint_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r∮C​F⋅dr around any closed loop?

    Answer
    000. You end where you started, so the height change is zero.
17.4

Green's theorem

Midterm 2

Chop the region into cells and spin each one counterclockwise. Along any wall between two cells, one cell pushes up and its neighbour pushes down — dead even. The only walls with nobody on the other side are on the outside.

circulation form ∮CP dx+Q dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA∮C​Pdx+Qdy=∬D​(∂x∂Q​−∂y∂P​)dA
flux (divergence) form — same theorem, rotated 90° ∮CF⋅n ds=∬D(∂P∂x+∂Q∂y)dA=∬Ddiv⁡F dA\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,ds = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y}\right)dA = \iint_D \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\ dA∮C​F⋅nds=∬D​(∂x∂P​+∂y∂Q​)dA=∬D​divF dA

Algorithm · apply Green's theorem

  1. Check the hypotheses. CCC must be closed, simple (no self-crossings), positively oriented — counterclockwise, region on your left — and F\mathbf FF smooth on all of DDD.
  2. Identify PPP and QQQ from ∮P dx+Q dy\oint P\,dx+Q\,dy∮Pdx+Qdy.
  3. Compute Qx−PyQ_x - P_yQx​−Py​ and simplify. This is usually far smaller than either piece.
  4. Set up ∬D\iint_D∬D​ over the enclosed region — polar if it's round.
  5. If CCC runs clockwise, apply the theorem anyway and negate the result.

Also runs backwards: a horrible double integral can become an easy loop integral. Read the problem for which direction is cheaper.

area for free — choose P and Q so that Qx−Py=1Q_x-P_y=1Qx​−Py​=1 A=∮Cx dy=−∮Cy dx=12∮Cx dy−y dxA = \oint_C x\,dy = -\oint_C y\,dx = \tfrac12\oint_C x\,dy - y\,dxA=∮C​xdy=−∮C​ydx=21​∮C​xdy−ydx

Algorithm · regions with a hole

  1. Orient both boundaries positively: outer curve counterclockwise, inner curve clockwise — so the region always stays on your left.
  2. Apply Green's theorem to the whole boundary C=Couter+CinnerC = C_{\text{outer}} + C_{\text{inner}}C=Couter​+Cinner​.
  3. If Qx−Py=0Q_x-P_y = 0Qx​−Py​=0 on the region between them, the two loop integrals are equal in magnitude — so you can replace a nasty outer curve with a tiny convenient circle around the hole.

That last trick is how the 2π2\pi2π in the 17.3 trap gets computed.

Check yourself

  1. Which way must CCC be oriented for Green's theorem?

    Answer
    Counterclockwise, region on your left. If it runs clockwise, apply the theorem anyway and negate.

  2. Give a line integral that returns the enclosed area.

    Answer
    A=∮Cx dyA=\oint_C x\,dyA=∮C​xdy (or −∮Cy dx-\oint_C y\,dx−∮C​ydx). Chosen so that Qx−Py=1Q_x-P_y=1Qx​−Py​=1.
17.5

Curl & divergence

Midterm 2

Curl: drop a paddlewheel in and see if it spins. Not "is the water going in a circle" — "is one side pushed harder than the other".

curl — a vector, computed as a determinant curl⁡F=∇×F=∣ijk∂∂x∂∂y∂∂zPQR∣\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F = \nabla\times\mathbf F = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\[2pt] \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}&\dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}&\dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}\\[6pt] P&Q&R\end{vmatrix}curlF=∇×F=​i∂x∂​P​j∂y∂​Q​k∂z∂​R​​

The direction of curl is the axis the paddlewheel spins about (right-hand rule); its length is how fast. In 2-D only the k\mathbf kk-component survives, and it is exactly the Qx−PyQ_x - P_yQx​−Py​ from Green's theorem.

Divergence: draw a tiny box. Count what flows in, count what flows out. More out than in means something inside is making it.

divergence — a scalar div⁡F=∇⋅F=∂P∂x+∂Q∂y+∂R∂z\operatorname{div}\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf F = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}divF=∇⋅F=∂x∂P​+∂y∂Q​+∂z∂R​

Two identities worth memorising outright

div⁡(curl⁡F)=0\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F) = 0div(curlF)=0 — a spin never creates anything.  curl⁡(∇f)=0\operatorname{curl}(\nabla f) = \mathbf 0curl(∇f)=0 — a hill never makes a whirlpool. Together they explain why a conservative field always has zero curl, and why a curl field always has zero flux out of a closed surface.

Type trap

curl of a vector field is a vector. Divergence of a vector field is a number. So div⁡(curl⁡F)\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F)div(curlF) makes sense and curl⁡(div⁡F)\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{div}\mathbf F)curl(divF) does not — you can't cross a scalar. Checking the type of your answer catches half of all algebra errors here.

Check yourself

  1. What is div⁡(curl⁡F)\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F)div(curlF)?

    Answer
    000, always. A spin never creates anything.

  2. What is curl⁡(∇f)\operatorname{curl}(\nabla f)curl(∇f)?

    Answer
    0\mathbf 00, always. A hill never makes a whirlpool.

  3. Is div⁡F\operatorname{div}\mathbf FdivF a scalar or a vector?

    Answer
    A scalar. So curl⁡(div⁡F)\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{div}\mathbf F)curl(divF) is not even defined — checking types catches half of all errors here.
17.6a

Parametric surfaces

Quiz 10

A surface is a rubber sheet with its own two coordinates. Move uuu a little and you slide one way; move vvv and you slide the other. Those two slides span a tiny tile — and 13.4 already told you its area.

tangent vectors, normal, and area element ru=∂r∂u,rv=∂r∂v,n dS=(ru×rv) du dv,dS=∣ru×rv∣ du dv\mathbf r_u = \frac{\partial\mathbf r}{\partial u},\quad \mathbf r_v = \frac{\partial\mathbf r}{\partial v},\qquad \mathbf n\,dS = (\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv, \qquad dS = |\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v|\,du\,dvru​=∂u∂r​,rv​=∂v∂r​,ndS=(ru​×rv​)dudv,dS=∣ru​×rv​∣dudv

The cross product does double duty: its direction is the surface normal, its length is the tile's area. Both things a surface integral needs, from one computation.

SurfaceParametrization∣ru×rv∣|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v|∣ru​×rv​∣
Graph z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y)⟨x, y, f(x,y)⟩\langle x,\ y,\ f(x,y)\rangle⟨x, y, f(x,y)⟩1+fx2+fy2\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}1+fx2​+fy2​​

Cone z=x2+y2z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}z=x2+y2​⟨rcos⁡θ, rsin⁡θ, r⟩\langle r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta,\ r\rangle⟨rcosθ, rsinθ, r⟩r2r\sqrt2r2​
Surface of revolution⟨x, f(x)cos⁡θ, f(x)sin⁡θ⟩\langle x,\ f(x)\cos\theta,\ f(x)\sin\theta\rangle⟨x, f(x)cosθ, f(x)sinθ⟩f1+(f′)2f\sqrt{1+(f')^2}f1+(f′)2​

Row 1 and row 2 are worth recognising instantly — they reproduce the surface-area formula from 17.6 and the ρ2sin⁡φ\rho^2\sin\varphiρ2sinφ from 16.5.

Check yourself

  1. What does (ru×rv) du dv(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv(ru​×rv​)dudv equal?

    Answer
    n dS\mathbf n\,dSndS — both the direction and the area, from one computation. Never normalise it and then also multiply by dSdSdS.
17.6b

Surface area

Quiz 10

Briggs files surface area under Surface Integrals (17.6) — which is why it sits here rather than back in Chapter 16.

A patch of hillside is always bigger than the flat patch beneath it. How much bigger depends on the tilt — and the tilt is exactly what the partial derivatives measure.

area of the graph of z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y) over the region RRR A(S)=∬R1+(fx)2+(fy)2 dAA(S) = \iint_R \sqrt{1 + \bigl(f_x\bigr)^2 + \bigl(f_y\bigr)^2}\ dAA(S)=∬R​1+(fx​)2+(fy​)2​ dA

Same shape as arc length, which was ∫1+(dy/dx)2 dx\int\sqrt{1+(dy/dx)^2}\,dx∫1+(dy/dx)2​dx — one dimension up. Flat ground gives fx=fy=0f_x=f_y=0fx​=fy​=0, the root becomes 1, and surface area collapses to plain area. That's your check.

Algorithm · surface area of a graph

  1. Solve for zzz so you have z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y).
  2. Compute fxf_xfx​ and fyf_yfy​, then 1+fx2+fy21+f_x^2+f_y^21+fx2​+fy2​ and simplify before integrating — this is usually where a clean root appears.
  3. Find RRR: the shadow of the surface on the xyxyxy-plane.
  4. Integrate over RRR, going polar if the shadow is round (it usually is).

For a surface given parametrically instead, jump to 17.6: A=∬∣ru×rv∣ dAA = \iint |\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v|\,dAA=∬∣ru​×rv​∣dA.

Check yourself

  1. What is the stretch factor for the graph z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y)z=f(x,y)?

    Answer
    1+fx2+fy2\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}1+fx2​+fy2​​.

  2. On flat ground, what does that factor become?

    Answer
    111, so surface area collapses to plain area. That is the check on every surface-area setup.
17.6c

Surface integrals & flux

Quiz 10

Hold a hoop in the wind. Facing it head-on you catch all of it. Turn it edge-on and you catch nothing — even though the wind hasn't changed. Only the part perpendicular to the surface gets through.

scalar surface integral — mass of a sheet ∬Sf dS=∬Df(r(u,v)) ∣ru×rv∣ du dv\iint_S f\,dS = \iint_D f\bigl(\mathbf r(u,v)\bigr)\,\bigl|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\bigr|\,du\,dv∬S​fdS=∬D​f(r(u,v))​ru​×rv​​dudv
flux of a vector field ∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅n dS=∬DF⋅(ru×rv) du dv\iint_S \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S = \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,dS = \iint_D \mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv∬S​F⋅dS=∬S​F⋅ndS=∬D​F⋅(ru​×rv​)dudv

Algorithm · compute a flux integral

  1. Parametrize SSS — use the table in 17.6 whenever it fits.
  2. Compute ru×rv\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_vru​×rv​. Do not normalise it and do not compute dSdSdS separately; the un-normalised cross product already carries both.
  3. Check orientation. Does the cross product point the way the problem wants (outward, upward)? If not, negate it.
  4. Substitute F\mathbf FF at the parametrized points, so everything is in uuu and vvv.
  5. Dot and integrate over the parameter region DDD.

For a graph z=g(x,y)z=g(x,y)z=g(x,y) oriented upward, this collapses to ∬D(−Pgx−Qgy+R)dA\iint_D\bigl(-P g_x - Q g_y + R\bigr)dA∬D​(−Pgx​−Qgy​+R)dA.

Orientation trap

Swapping uuu and vvv flips the normal, and flipping the normal negates your flux. Always sanity-check by evaluating the normal at one concrete point: for a sphere with outward orientation it should point away from the origin.

Check yourself

  1. You turn the net edge-on to the wind. How much gets through?

    Answer
    Nothing. F⊥n\mathbf F\perp\mathbf nF⊥n makes F⋅n=0\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n=0F⋅n=0, even though the wind never changed.

  2. Should you normalise ru×rv\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_vru​×rv​ before dotting with F\mathbf FF?

    Answer
    No. The raw cross product already carries dSdSdS inside it.
17.7

Stokes' theorem

Final Exam

Dip a bent wire loop in soap. The film can be flat or bulge out like a bubble. Both have the same rim, so both have the same total spin through them. Pick the lazy one.

circulation around the rim = curl through any surface it bounds ∮CF⋅dr=∬S(curl⁡F)⋅dS\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_S (\operatorname{curl}\mathbf F)\cdot d\mathbf S∮C​F⋅dr=∬S​(curlF)⋅dS

Algorithm · use Stokes' theorem

  1. Decide which side is easier. Nasty curve, simple curl → go right. Nasty surface, simple curve → go left.
  2. Choose the friendliest surface with that rim. A flat disk or the plane region inside CCC almost always beats the surface you were handed.
  3. Compute curl⁡F\operatorname{curl}\mathbf FcurlF as a determinant.
  4. Match orientations by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of your right hand along CCC, and your thumb must point the way n\mathbf nn points. Mismatch = wrong sign.
  5. Evaluate the surface integral using 17.6.

Green's theorem is exactly this with the surface lying flat in the xyxyxy-plane and n=k\mathbf n = \mathbf kn=k.

Check yourself

  1. You are told SSS is 'any smooth surface with boundary CCC'. Does the choice matter?

    Answer
    No. Only the rim matters — pick the laziest surface, usually the flat disk.

  2. When is Green's theorem just Stokes' theorem?

    Answer
    When the surface lies flat in the xyxyxy-plane with n=k\mathbf n=\mathbf kn=k. Same theorem, tilted.
17.8

The divergence theorem

Final Exam

Fill a solid with tiny cubes. Whatever leaks out the right face of one cube leaks into the left face of the next. Every internal face cancels with its partner. The only faces with nothing behind them are on the outer skin.

flux out of a closed surface = divergence inside ∯SF⋅dS=∭Ediv⁡F dV\oiint_S \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S = \iiint_E \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\ dV∬​S​F⋅dS=∭E​divF dV

Algorithm · use the divergence theorem

  1. Confirm SSS is closed — a sealed bag with no openings — and oriented outward.
  2. Compute div⁡F=Px+Qy+Rz\operatorname{div}\mathbf F = P_x+Q_y+R_zdivF=Px​+Qy​+Rz​. This is usually startlingly simple compared to F\mathbf FF itself.
  3. Set up ∭E\iiint_E∭E​ over the enclosed solid, in whichever coordinates match it (16.4–16.5).
  4. Integrate. Often div⁡F\operatorname{div}\mathbf FdivF is a constant, and the answer is just that constant times the volume.

Algorithm · when the surface is NOT closed

  1. Cap it. Add a simple surface S2S_2S2​ (usually a flat disk) to seal the opening.
  2. Apply the theorem to the sealed union: ∯S∪S2=∭Ediv⁡F dV\displaystyle\oiint_{S\cup S_2} = \iiint_E \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\,dV∬​S∪S2​​=∭E​divFdV.
  3. Compute the cap's flux separately — it's flat, so it's easy.
  4. Subtract: ∬S=∭Ediv⁡F dV−∬S2\displaystyle\iint_S = \iiint_E \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\,dV - \iint_{S_2}∬S​=∭E​divFdV−∬S2​​.
  5. Watch the cap's orientation: as part of the sealed bag it must point outward, which for a bottom cap means downward.

This capping trick is the single most-tested idea on the final.

Check yourself

  1. What two conditions must SSS satisfy?

    Answer
    It must be closed (a sealed bag) and oriented outward.

  2. The surface is open. Now what?

    Answer
    Cap it, apply the theorem to the sealed union, compute the cap's flux separately, then subtract it. The cap must point outward too.
17 ·

The punchline: all five are one theorem

What happens on the edge equals what the derivative does inside. The only thing that changes between them is how many dimensions you're in.

TheoremStatementThe "inside"Its edge
FTC∫abf′ dx=f(b)−f(a)\int_a^b f'\,dx = f(b)-f(a)∫ab​f′dx=f(b)−f(a)an interval2 endpoints
FTLI∫C∇f⋅dr=f(B)−f(A)\int_C \nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r = f(B)-f(A)∫C​∇f⋅dr=f(B)−f(A)a curve2 endpoints
Green∮CF⋅dr=∬D(Qx−Py) dA\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_D (Q_x-P_y)\,dA∮C​F⋅dr=∬D​(Qx​−Py​)dAa flat regionone loop
Stokes∮CF⋅dr=∬Scurl⁡F⋅dS\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_S \operatorname{curl}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S∮C​F⋅dr=∬S​curlF⋅dSa surfaceits rim
Divergence∯SF⋅dS=∭Ediv⁡F dV\oiint_S \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf S = \iiint_E \operatorname{div}\mathbf F\,dV∬​S​F⋅dS=∭E​divFdVa solidits skin

If you remember one thing

Derivatives measure local change. Integrals add local change up. When you add up local change over a whole region, everything in the middle cancels with its neighbour and you're left standing on the boundary. That is the entire second half of Calc III.

Check yourself

  1. Say all four theorems in one sentence.

    Answer
    What happens on the edge equals what the derivative does inside. Everything in the middle cancels with its neighbour.

  2. You have a horrible closed-surface flux integral. First thought?

    Answer
    Divergence theorem — compute div⁡F\operatorname{div}\mathbf FdivF first. It is usually startlingly simpler than F\mathbf FF.

Every formula in this course is a sentence about a picture. When a problem looks unfamiliar, don't reach for the formula — reach for the picture, and ask what it's doing. Where does the arrow point? What cancels? What's left on the edge?
